newsitem.title: INDIA: Pro-autonomy party wins Kashmir vote, woos rebels.
newsitem.headline: Pro-autonomy party wins Kashmir vote, woos rebels.

text.p: The largest pro-India party in troubled Kashmir won a sweeping majority in the first local elections in the state since a separatist revolt began in 1990 and quickly offered an olive branch to rebels.
The moderate National Conference party, led by former chief minister Farooq Abdullah, won 54 seats in the Jammu and Kashmir state's 87-member assembly, results showed on Wednesday.
Counting in the six remaining constituencies that went to the polls over the weekend was to start on Thursday.

Abdullah, who has lambasted separatists as Pakistani agents through the years, stuck to a tough line against militancy but offered to meet leaders of the All-Parties Hurriyat (freedom) Conference, which bands some 30 separatist groups.
"I think we will continue to fight the renegades, the Pakistani infiltrators," he told Reuters, but added: "I hope they will come round and we will talk to each other.
"Finally we all have to live there. And we would like to bring them round to thinking in terms of the constitution of India," he said.
"We are particularly hopeful that our plank of enlargement of autonomy has been accepted by the people," Saifuddin Soz, National Conference spokesman, told Reuters.
Analysts see a battle ahead for Abdullah, who has been seen in his two previous tenures as chief minister as having failed to juggle Kashmiri feelings and India's federal policies.
He was the chief minister when the separatist rebellion erupted. More than 20,000 people have died during the revolt in mainly Hindu India's only Moslem-majority province.
India's constitution gave Kashmiris control over most affairs, but New Delhi has since 1952 gradually eroded these powers, which Abdullah wants to restore.
Among the powers was the right for Kashmir to have its own Wazir-e-Azam, or prime minister. Soz said he hoped Abdullah would eventually take the oath as prime minister.
"On October 6, we shall have a legislature party meeting, and then on October 8, he will be sworn in as chief minister, and Inshallah (God willing), later as Wazir-e-Azam," Soz said.

With 81 of 87 races decided, the National Conference had a commanding lead over its rivals. The Congress party and Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) each had seven seats, and Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's Janata Dal party had five.

Members of the separatist Hurriyat said Abdullah's victory would not help solve Kashmir's problems. "Unless you address the people's basic aspirations for self-determination, you cannot do much," Hurriyat member Abdul Majid Banday said.
Abdullah has rejected the separatists' demand for independence or merger with Pakistan.
India accuses Pakistan, which rules over a third of disputed Kashmir, of arming the separatists. Islamabad denies the charge, saying it extends them only moral and political support.
Abdullah's party boycotted parliamentary polls held earlier this year, saying the Congress government of then prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao would not give autonomy to Kashmir.
India was accused of coercing people to vote during that election, but the allegations were largely absent during last month's polls.

"By participating in the elections in large numbers, the people of Jammu and Kashmir have not only elected a government of their choice, but have also shown where their heart lies," Deve Gowda said in a statement on Wednesday.

After Deve Gowda assumed power in June, his centre-left United Front coalition pledged "maximum autonomy" to Jammu and Kashmir. Abdullah said on Wednesday his party was ready to join the United Front.
